title: Grade 10 Mathematics — Probability
description: Probability — theoretical, cards, dice, bags of balls, complementary events (CBSE Ch. 15)
subject: mathematics

questions.question: The theoretical probability of an event E is defined as:
options: P(E) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of equally likely outcomes
questions.explanation: Theoretical (classical) probability: P(E) = Number of outcomes favourable to E / Total number of equally likely outcomes. This assumes all outcomes are equally likely.

questions.question: The probability of any event E always satisfies:
questions.explanation: Probability is always between 0 and 1 (inclusive). P(E) = 0 means the event is impossible; P(E) = 1 means the event is certain (sure event).

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed once. The probability of getting a tail is:
questions.explanation: A fair coin has 2 equally likely outcomes: Head (H) and Tail (T). Favourable outcomes for tail = 1. P(Tail) = 1/2.

questions.question: A fair die (numbered 1 to 6) is rolled once. The probability of getting an even number is:
questions.explanation: Even numbers on a die: {2, 4, 6} → 3 favourable outcomes. Total outcomes = 6. P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.question: A fair die is rolled. The probability of getting a prime number is:
questions.explanation: Prime numbers on a die: {2, 3, 5} → 3 favourable outcomes. Total outcomes = 6. P(prime) = 3/6 = 1/2.

questions.question: From a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards, one card is drawn at random. The probability that it is a king is:
questions.explanation: There are 4 kings in a deck of 52 cards (one per suit). P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13.

questions.question: From a deck of 52 cards, one card is drawn. The probability that it is a face card (Jack, Queen, or King) is:
questions.explanation: Face cards are Jack, Queen, and King — 3 per suit × 4 suits = 12 face cards. P(face card) = 12/52 = 3/13.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 red balls, 5 blue balls, and 2 white balls. A ball is drawn at random. The probability of drawing a red ball is:
If P(E) = 3/7, then P(E̅) — the probability of E NOT occurring — is:
questions.explanation: P(E̅) = 1 − P(E) = 1 − 3/7 = 4/7. The sum of probabilities of an event and its complement always equals 1.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed simultaneously. The probability of getting exactly two heads is:
questions.explanation: Sample space for two coins: {HH, HT, TH, TT} — 4 equally likely outcomes. Favourable (HH) = 1. P(HH) = 1/4.

questions.question: A bag contains 4 red, 6 blue, and 2 white balls. The probability of drawing a ball that is NOT red is:
questions.explanation: Total balls = 4 + 6 + 2 = 12. Not red = 6 + 2 = 8. P(not red) = 8/12 = 2/3. Alternatively, P(not red) = 1 − P(red) = 1 − 4/12 = 8/12 = 2/3.

questions.question: From a deck of 52 cards, one card is drawn. The probability of getting a card that is neither a heart nor a king is:
questions.explanation: Hearts = 13; Kings = 4 (but King of Hearts already counted). Cards that are a heart OR a king = 13 + 4 − 1 = 16. Cards that are neither = 52 − 16 = 36. P = 36/52 = 9/13.

questions.question: The probability of an impossible event is:
questions.explanation: An impossible event has no favourable outcomes. P(impossible) = 0/Total outcomes = 0. For example, getting a 7 on a standard die is impossible — P = 0.

From a deck of 52 cards, a card is drawn at random. The probability that it is a spade is:
questions.explanation: There are 13 spades in a deck of 52 cards. P(spade) = 13/52 = 1/4. A deck has 4 suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs) with 13 cards each.
